claims.text: Sluggish atomic diffusion, rather than configurational entropy, is the predominant factor governing structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
Reduced atomic mobility limits grain-boundary segregation.
Reduced atomic mobility limits nanoprecipitate evolution.
Limiting segregation and nanoprecipitate evolution maintains a stable disordered solid solution.
Samples with identical elemental compositions have similar configurational entropy.
Changing grain size systematically modulates effective atomic diffusion kinetics.
Trace isotopic markers can differentiate and track atomic diffusion rates.
The range 800–1000°C is relevant to high-temperature structural applications of high-entropy alloys.
Diffusion-driven processes are activated during exposure at 800–1000°C.
High-entropy alloy microstructures can contain nanoprecipitates and both ordered and disordered solid-solution phases.
Grain boundaries and nanoprecipitates form through diffusion-mediated atomic rearrangements.
High configurational entropy favors a disordered solid solution.
Lower diffusion activity stabilizes the alloy against chemical inhomogeneity and microstructural coarsening.
Finer grain sizes lower effective atomic diffusivity in the proposed samples.
Isotope modification lowers effective atomic diffusivity in the proposed samples.
Samples with lower effective diffusivity will show less phase separation, grain-boundary segregation, and nanoprecipitate formation than the baseline.
Reduced phase separation, segregation, and precipitation will improve retention of structural integrity and chemical homogeneity at high temperature.
Outside 800–1000°C or under aggressive chemical environments, mechanisms other than diffusion may dominate stability.
The magnitude of diffusion-related stability improvement depends on alloy composition and processing details.
A lack of statistically significant reductions in segregation and nanoprecipitate formation in Group A relative to Group B would falsify the proposed primary-mechanism hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention initially describes isotopic markers as tools for differentiating and tracking diffusion, but the prediction and experimental design treat isotope modification or tracer techniques as interventions that slow diffusion. These are distinct roles, so the identity of the actual diffusion-modifying intervention is internally inconsistent.
